title: Elihu: God Speaks in Dreams and in Pain
summary: Elihu turns from the three friends to Job himself. He quotes Job's claim to be innocent and his complaint that God treats him as an enemy and never answers, and he replies that God does speak: through warning dreams at night and through sickness that brings a person near death. If a messenger, a mediator, stands beside such a sufferer and God finds a ransom, the person is restored, confesses his sin, and sings of his rescue.
story: Elihu, the young man introduced in chapter 32 as Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, has waited while his elders spoke and has grown angry with all of them: with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and with the three friends for condemning Job without answering him. Chapter 33 is the heart of his first speech. Job had repeatedly demanded that God answer him and had longed for someone to stand between them (9:33, 16:19-21). Elihu takes up both complaints. He offers himself as a fellow creature of clay who will not overwhelm Job, and he argues that God has not been silent at all. His four speeches (chapters 32 to 37) stand between Job's final oath of innocence in chapter 31 and the LORD's answer from the whirlwind in chapter 38.
historical:
Like the rest of Job, the chapter is set in a patriarchal world outside Israel, in the land of Uz, and it can't be tied to a datable event. Elihu's family name links him to Buz, a name that appears in Genesis 22:21 among the relatives of Abraham and in Jeremiah 25:23 among the desert peoples of Arabia, which fits the book's setting on the eastern fringe of the Israelite world.

The Elihu speeches raise a literary-historical question. Elihu isn't mentioned in the prologue or in the epilogue, where God rebukes the three friends but says nothing of him, and his style differs somewhat from the rest of the poem. Many critical scholars think his speeches were added by a later writer who wanted to supply an answer the original dialogue lacked. Others, including many conservative scholars and a number of literary critics, argue that the speeches were part of the design from the start, deliberately placed to delay God's answer and to test yet another human explanation before God speaks. Readers on both sides take the speeches seriously as part of the book as it stands.
cultural:
Elihu's opening appeal rests on customs of honor and age. In the ancient Near East the old spoke first and the young listened, which is why he says in chapter 32 that he waited. Having broken that order, he works hard to justify speaking, and he claims authority not from age but from the breath of the Almighty that gives life to every person (33:4). His picture of God speaking in dreams draws on a belief shared across the ancient world, where dreams were widely treated as channels of divine warning. Eliphaz had already described a terrifying night vision in 4:12-17, and Elihu develops the idea in a gentler direction: the dream is a warning meant to turn a person back from pride.

His second picture, the sick man wasting away until he nears the Pit, reflects a world without modern medicine, where serious illness was routinely life-threatening and was often read as a sign of God's displeasure. The Pit is a common Old Testament name for the grave and the realm of the dead. The idea of a heavenly advocate who pleads for a mortal also had parallels in the region, where people imagined personal gods or protective spirits interceding with the great gods on their behalf.
literary: The chapter is built as a formal address. Verses 1 to 7 are a lengthy preface in which Elihu calls for attention and describes his own sincerity, a feature some readers find pompous and others find courteous. Verses 8 to 11 quote Job's own words back to him, drawing on his earlier speeches (compare 13:24, 13:27). Verses 12 to 30 are the argument proper, built around two ways God speaks: the night dream (verses 14 to 18) and the sickbed (verses 19 to 28). The second is developed into a small drama, from suffering to the appearance of a mediating messenger, to restoration, to a song of thanks sung before others. Verses 29 and 30 summarize, and verses 31 to 33 close with an invitation that also shuts Job out: speak if you can, and if not, be quiet and learn.

outline.t: Elihu asks Job to listen as one creature of clay to another
God speaks in dreams to turn people from pride
God speaks through sickness that brings a person near death
The mediating messenger, the ransom, and the song of the restored
God's purpose to bring back the soul, and a call to listen

doctrines.note: Elihu insists that God is not silent: he speaks in one way and in another, though people fail to notice. The chapter widens the idea of how God addresses human beings to include warnings in the night and the experience of suffering itself.

Elihu moves beyond the friends' view that suffering is simply punishment. For him, pain can be discipline with a merciful purpose, meant to turn a person back before it is too late. The book will not let this become a full explanation of Job's case, but it names something many sufferers have recognized.

The messenger who says, “Spare him from going down to the Pit; I have found his ransom” gives a glimpse of rescue that comes from outside the sufferer: God's gracious provision of a payment that releases a life under sentence.

words.note: Luts, whose basic sense is to scorn or mock. In a special form of the verb, its participle means an interpreter or go-between, someone who speaks for another (Genesis 42:23 uses it for the interpreter between Joseph and his brothers). That is its sense in verse 23, where it is translated mediator. Job had lamented that there was no mediator between him and God (9:33); Elihu describes one.

Kopher, ransom. The word means a price paid to release a life that would otherwise be forfeit, as in Exodus 21:30 and 30:12. It is closely related to the verb used for making atonement. In verse 24 the ransom is found for the sufferer, not produced by him (whether the speaker who finds it is the messenger or God is left unclear), which makes the rescue an act of grace.

Malak, messenger, the same word used for angels and for human envoys. Here it is a messenger who stands on the sufferer's side, one in a thousand. Interpreters debate whether Elihu means an angel, a human teacher who explains God's ways, or a figure left deliberately undefined. The word itself allows each.

Shachat, the Pit, a name for the grave and the realm of death. It appears five times in this chapter (verses 18, 22, 24, 28, 30), and the repetition is the backbone of the argument: God's warnings and disciplines aim to keep a person from going down to the Pit and to bring him back to the light.

christ: Job had longed for someone who could stand between him and God, and Elihu sketches that figure: a messenger on the sufferer's side, a mediator who declares what is right, and a ransom that spares a life from the Pit. Elihu isn't predicting the Messiah, and the passage should not be read as a coded prophecy. But the pattern it describes, a go-between who pleads for the dying and a ransom provided by God himself, is exactly what the New Testament says has come in Jesus. Paul calls him the one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:5-6), and Jesus described his own death as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). What Job and Elihu could only imagine, the gospel announces as done.

hard.q: Is Elihu right, or is he just one more friend who misjudges Job?
hard.a:
Readers have divided sharply. Some see Elihu as a brash young man who promises something new and delivers largely what the friends already said: that Job is at fault and should submit. They note that he quotes Job's words selectively and that God never commends him. Others see him as a genuine advance. He doesn't claim Job's suffering proves past sin; he argues that suffering can be God's merciful warning and discipline, and his closing speeches on God's greatness in the storm lead directly into God's own speech. On this view, the silence about Elihu at the end means he is not rebuked with the friends.

A fair reading holds both. Elihu corrects the friends' mechanical view and says true things about God's patience and purposes. Yet he still doesn't know what the reader knows from the prologue, that Job was tested precisely because he was blameless. Whatever is true in his account, it cannot be the whole answer to Job's case.

questions: Elihu says God speaks in one way and in another, yet no one notices. What might it look like to pay attention to ways God speaks that you've overlooked?
Elihu treats pain as possible discipline meant to turn a person back. When is that a comforting truth, and when does it become a cruel thing to say to someone who is suffering?
Job longed for a mediator, and Elihu describes one. What difference does it make to you that the New Testament names Jesus as that mediator and ransom?
